title: Name the Triangle
statement:
You get an array sides of exactly three positive integers, in no particular order. Decide what triangle they make and return one of these strings:

  • "none" if the three lengths cannot form a triangle at all,
  • "equilateral" if all three sides are equal,
  • "isosceles" if exactly two sides are equal,
  • "scalene" if all three are different.

Three lengths form a triangle only when each one is strictly shorter than the sum of the other two. Lengths that just reach (a flat, zero-area shape) do not count.

examples.why: 5 + 5 = 10 > 8, so it is a triangle, and exactly two sides match.
Two sides match, but 2 + 2 = 4 is not more than 9. Checking only for equal sides would wrongly say isosceles.
3 + 4 = 7 exactly. The shape would be a flat line, which is not a triangle.

hints: Check two things, in the right order. Which one has to come first?
Validity first: an equal pair says nothing about whether the lengths close up into a triangle.
Sort the three lengths. Then the only inequality that can fail is smallest + middle > largest, and the number of distinct values names the type.

explain.intuition:
Three sticks close into a triangle only if each is shorter than the other two together. After sorting, the two shorter sticks are the only pair that could fall short, so a single check a + b > c covers all three conditions.

Once you know it is a triangle, the name only depends on how many distinct lengths there are: one, two or three. The order matters: test validity before equality, or [2, 2, 9] gets called isosceles.
steps: Sort the sides so that a ≤ b ≤ c.
If a === c, all three are equal: return "equilateral".
If a === b or b === c, return "isosceles"; otherwise return "scalene".
pitfalls: Naming the shape before checking it is a triangle at all.
Using ≥ in the triangle test. When a + b === c the shape is flat and does not count.
Checking only one inequality without sorting first, so a long side in the first position slips through.

solutions.title: All three inequalities, then count equal pairs
solutions.idea: Test each side against the sum of the other two, then compare the sides pairwise.

solutions.title: Sort, one inequality, count distinct
solutions.idea: After sorting only the two short sides can fail to reach the long one. The number of distinct lengths gives the name.

followups: Also say whether the triangle is right, acute or obtuse.
Given n stick lengths, count how many triples form a valid triangle.
